owner: xlog baseline — mainstream shorts conventions + pilot creator references (v4: LoL commentary/subtitle-sync; v5: cinematic movie-recap, subtitle color/size/sync)

criteria.name: hook_strength
criteria.description: The opening must stop the scroll immediately: cold-open on the highest-action / highest-emotion moment with no title card, logo, self-introduction, or pre-roll, and land the first caption line within the first ~0.5s. Three accepted hook forms: (a) an unresolved claim or question that only completes in the next line, (b) a bold, complete thesis claim ('this champion is the strongest late-game top') stated over already-in-progress action that the footage immediately proves, or (c) a premise sentence split across the first two shots so the payoff clause arrives only after the first cut. For live-action or cinematic footage, the 0s frame should be the most recognizable image available — a peak-emotion or iconic character close-up with visible physical evidence (blood, bruise, grip, tears) beats a detail/object insert. Judged over the first 3 seconds.

criteria.name: mainstream_convention
criteria.description: Follows proven, broadly appealing Shorts/Reels conventions for caption placement, structure, and readability. Safe beats experimental — except that the creator's references establish two accepted house forms: (1) narration-subtitle-driven gameplay commentary and (2) cinematic recap built from tight close-ups in a shot/reverse-shot dialogue rhythm. Do not penalize on their own a centered vertical crop that keeps the game HUD readable, 16:9-in-9:16 letterboxing, heavy zoom/reframing of source footage, or a persistent watermark/anchor element. Shot lengths of 3–5s are acceptable and expected in narration-led gameplay when each shot carries new visible information and cuts land on sentence boundaries; sub-2s cutting is equally acceptable in dialogue-driven recap when every cut coincides with a caption change. Color-coded caption text is conventional here, not experimental, as long as contrast and legibility hold.

criteria.name: instruction_fit
criteria.description: Faithfully realizes the user's free-form request (caption tone, effects, mood, color scheme). When the brief asks for subtitles, near-every-beat captioning is expected and a run of silent shots is a real miss — but deliberate short caption gaps (0.5–1.5s) during narration pauses, in-game banners, or the peak beat are intentional craft, not a miss. Requested caption color/size conventions must be applied consistently across the whole video rather than shot by shot. Ignore this criterion (redistribute judgment) when no request was given.

criteria.name: pacing
criteria.description: No dead air and energy rising toward the payoff. Perceived pace is caption-led, and caption/audio sync is the primary pacing lever: text that leads the audio or lingers past it is a defect even if the cut rhythm is good. Two valid rhythms. (1) Narration-led: subtitles swap exactly on spoken clause boundaries (each caption held ~2–4s) and cuts land on sentence boundaries with shots running ~3–5s. (2) Dialogue-led: a cut or a new push-in lands on every caption change, average shot length under ~2s through the first 15s, then holds stretch to 2–3s for the emotional turn with captions swapping inside the held shot, and the last few seconds settle into near-static close-ups with sparse text. In both, caption in/out points should hit the exact spoken syllable. Deliberate rhythm breaks (a mid-roll still interlude, one caption-free breath before the payoff) are welcome when they set up a payoff. Tighter cutting alone does not outrank a clearer, better-grounded arc.

criteria.name: narrative_clarity
criteria.description: One clear thread from hook to payoff; no confusing jumps. The strongest shape is question → clue → reveal: the hook poses a question or thesis, each following shot releases one new visible clue, and the payoff answers it with a concrete detail rather than restating the premise. Documentary or narration captions must be anchored to something actually visible in the frame — inferred or atmospheric assertions the footage does not show are a clarity defect, not a stylistic choice; captions that transcribe spoken dialogue are exempt, but then the speaker must be unambiguous (visible face, shot/reverse-shot, or a consistent per-speaker text color). Continuity aids — one dominant color grade and slow push-ins across hard cuts — count toward clarity when they make a jumpy assembly read as one scene. Silent visual interludes are fine when they restate the narration's point rather than introduce a new one.

criteria.name: moment_selection
criteria.description: The genuinely best raw moments were used, not filler. Prefer shots that contain concrete, readable evidence (faces at peak emotion, iconic recognizable frames, hands, marks, revealed names/objects, HUD gold/level/item state) over connective coverage such as low-angle feet, wide walking, or empty-space shots. Tight close-ups on the speaking or reacting face are preferred over wides during dialogue beats.

preferences: Open cold on the most recognizable peak-action or peak-emotion close-up with the first caption inside 0.5 seconds — a thesis claim the footage instantly proves, an unresolved claim, or a premise sentence split across the first two shots — with no intro, logo, or self-introduction.

For live-action narrative footage, structure the edit as question → clue → reveal: hook on a peak-emotion face close-up that poses the question, release one new visible clue per shot, and pay it off with a concrete detail shot that answers it.

Caption only what is literally visible in the frame (a bruise, a hand gripping an arm, a name tattooed on skin) unless the caption is transcribing spoken dialogue, and avoid interpretive or atmospheric lines the footage does not show.
Choose footage that literally demonstrates the sentence being narrated, and order clips chronologically (early game → late game, or story order) so the argument escalates toward the payoff.
In narration-led edits, cut only on sentence or clause boundaries so every shot change coincides with a new narration line, keeping shots roughly 3–5 seconds.
In dialogue-driven edits, cut on every caption change so each new line lands on a new shot or a new push-in, keeping average shot length under 2 seconds through the first 15 seconds.
Cut dialogue exchanges as shot/reverse-shot close-ups that alternate faces on each beat.
Slow to 2–3 second holds on a single face for the emotional turn and let captions swap inside the held shot.
Time every caption's in and out point to the exact spoken syllable or clause boundary, holding narration lines 2–4 seconds, and never let text appear before the audio or linger past it.
Carry a continuing line unchanged across a cut instead of retyping or dropping it.

Show one short line of text at a time (about 6–10 characters or a single clause) for dialogue, and cap narration captions at two lines of roughly 8–16 characters broken at natural grammatical phrase points.

Assign a fixed caption color per speaker or emotion (yellow = protagonist/main narrator, pale blue = the other voice, red = threat or refusal, green = magic or twist, off-white = neutral narration) and keep that mapping consistent for the entire video.
Burn captions as bold rounded sans-serif with a heavy dark outline or soft dark glow/drop shadow, hard-cut in and out with no animation.

Place captions centered horizontally at about 50–55% of frame height over the chest or chin and never over the subject's eyes for face-driven footage, and in the lower third above the HUD — never covering the minimap, item bar, or scoreboard — for gameplay.

Insert deliberate 0.5–1.5s caption gaps during narration pauses, whenever the footage shows its own banner or title (kill, tower, level-up), and on the peak action beat so the on-screen event reads cleanly.
Pin one persistent identity element for the whole video — a subject or topic icon at top-center, or a lyric/music watermark along the bottom.
Frame 9:16 either by cropping vertically with the subject centered or by letterboxing the 16:9 image, keeping the HUD readable and using any black bars as caption space.
Grade every clip toward one dominant color wash and add a slow digital push-in inside each static shot so hard cuts read as one continuous scene.
When the brief asks for subtitles, keep a caption on nearly every beat and reserve silence for the planned gaps and the final loop cut.
Insert one silent full-bleed meme/still interlude around the 55–70% mark that visually restates the narration's joke, holding each still 2–3 seconds.
Join interlude stills with 0.5–1s dip-to-black fades rather than hard cuts, and drop all captions during the interlude so the image carries the gag.
End on a final decisive clip or a single quiet close-up — a takeaway generalization, a short self-deprecating reaction, or a wordless emotional button — with no outro card or CTA.
Avoid emojis and on-screen title cards.
notes: v5 — merged the pilot creator's second reference short https://youtube.com/shorts/jTXmdpVkq-A?si=VJr65PE6eSuKFTLj (Korean cinematic movie-recap, ~41s, tight close-ups of two characters cut shot/reverse-shot, magenta/purple grade, slow push-in on every shot, persistent 'BURN IT UP' lyric watermark over a music bed). Creator note: '영상의 자막의 색과 크기, 싱크가 잘 맞음. 학습' — what to learn is caption COLOR, SIZE, and SYNC. What the reference taught: one short line at a time (~6–10 chars), bold rounded Korean sans-serif, centered horizontally at ~50–55% frame height over chest/chin and never over the eyes; a fixed color-per-speaker/emotion mapping (yellow protagonist, pale blue other voice, red threat/refusal, green magic/twist, off-white narrator) held for the whole video; soft dark glow/drop shadow behind all text for legibility over bright busy faces; caption in/out timed to the exact spoken syllable, with a continuing line carried unchanged across a cut; a cut or push-in on every caption change (sub-2s average in the first 15s), stretching to 2–3s holds for the emotional turn and near-static sparse-text close-ups for the landing; cold open on the most recognizable action image with the premise sentence split across the first two shots; one dominant color grade plus slow digital zoom to make hard cuts feel continuous; no outro card or CTA. Criterion edits made only where this reference contradicted v4: hook_strength gained the split-premise-across-first-two-shots form; pacing now describes two valid rhythms (narration-led 3–5s shots with 2–4s captions, and dialogue-led sub-2s cutting on every caption change) and upgrades sync precision from clause-level to syllable-level; mainstream_convention now accepts sub-2s dialogue cutting, heavy zoom/reframing, and color-coded caption text alongside the v4 gameplay form; narrative_clarity exempts transcribed dialogue from the 'must be visible in frame' rule (while requiring unambiguous speaker attribution) and credits grade+push-in continuity; moment_selection now names iconic recognizable frames and prefers close-ups over wides on dialogue beats; instruction_fit adds consistency of requested caption color/size. Weights unchanged — both references point at the same subtitle-craft core, so no rebalancing was warranted. Preferences: the v4 'bold white text' spec was generalized into a color-mapping rule plus a separate outline/glow rule; the caption placement rule now covers both face-driven centering at 50–55% height and gameplay lower-third-above-HUD; the line-length rule now allows one 6–10 char dialogue line; six new rules added (cut-on-every-caption-change for dialogue edits, shot/reverse-shot alternation, 2–3s holds for the emotional turn, syllable-exact sync merged with the v4 clause-sync rule, carry-a-line-across-a-cut, unified color grade + slow push-in); the identity-anchor rule was widened from a top-center icon to include a bottom lyric/music watermark; the ending rule now also allows a wordless emotional button. All v4 gameplay-commentary and live-action-documentary rules retained since this reference did not contradict them.
